tier_reason: Tier B kept because HPTT is the subject of a peer-reviewed ARRAY 2017 paper (Springer, Su, Bientinesi). The paper could not be opened in the 2026-10-02 retier pass: arXiv, ACM DL, sigplan.org, alphaxiv.org, huggingface.co and Semantic Scholar are egress-blocked, and no copy exists in springer13's GitHub repositories. The claimed_speedup field now holds only what was seen: the README's numpy figure and the paper's Fig. 6 (benchmark/bw.png in the repo). The 'up to 27.4x vs Eigen' figure appeared again only in a search-result summary, so it moves to caveats as unverified.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Seen on opened pages only. README figure misc/hptt_vs_numpy.png (bar chart, values read by eye): 57 test cases, HPTT on 24 threads of 2x Xeon E5-2680 v3 against numpy.transpose(A, perm).copy(), about 5.1x (case 46) to about 19.7x (case 42), most cases between 7x and 13x. benchmark/bw.png (the paper's Fig. 6): HPTT bandwidth over 57 cases with and without autotuning is at or near the system SAXPY and STREAM lines on Ivy Bridge (about 23-39 GiB/s against SAXPY about 35 GiB/s), KNL, IBM Power7, AMD and ARM. No library baseline appears in that figure.
corrections.baseline: numpy.transpose (np.transpose(A, perm).copy(order=order) in pythonAPI/benchmark/benchmark.py) is the only baseline seen with numbers. The ARRAY 2017 paper reportedly compares against Eigen's tensor transposition (Eigen::Tensor shuffle), but that is known only from its abstract as quoted by search results; the paper was not opened.
corrections.caveats: The paper's headline claims come from its abstract as reproduced by search-result summaries (seen in the 2026-09-26 and 2026-10-02 passes): up to 27.4x faster than Eigen's tensor transposition, bandwidth comparable to SAXPY across Ivy Bridge, ARMv7 and IBM Power7, and up to 3.1x faster tensor contractions once HPTT is integrated into CTF. The paper itself (arXiv 1704.04374, DOI 10.1145/3091966.3091968) could not be opened, so the Eigen ratio, its CPU, compiler, thread count and per-case spread are unverified. The repo has no Eigen harness: benchmark/benchmark.cpp compares only with an in-repo naive OpenMP reference transposition and optionally the original TTC. The README's numpy comparison runs HPTT on 24 threads against a numpy copy whose thread count is not stated (numpy's copy is normally single-threaded), so the 5-20x range mostly reflects multi-threaded bandwidth use. HPTT also applies alpha/beta while the numpy side only copies, and the figure values are read by eye. The current Python benchmark allocates float64 arrays whatever --floatType says. The repository has been unmaintained since 2022. A transposition library is BLAS-adjacent rather than a BLAS/LAPACK routine, so the category is a loose fit.

tier_reason: Tier C stays: AMGCL's own author ran the comparison. The benchmark code is public (ddemidov/amgcl_benchmarks has the shared- and distributed-memory Poisson and Navier-Stokes harnesses for AMGCL, PETSc, Trilinos ML and CUSP), the raw timings are public (docs/smem_data, docs/dmem_data in the amgcl repo), and the CPUs are named (dual Xeon E5-2640 v3; Xeon Platinum 8160, E5-2690 v3 and E5-2697 v3 on the clusters). But no compiler, compiler version, optimization flags, build type or PETSc/Trilinos/CUDA versions are recorded in amgcl_benchmarks or in docs/benchmarks.rst, so the A criteria are not met.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. The public harness (ddemidov/amgcl_benchmarks, top-level CMakeLists.txt) sets only C++11 plus the OpenMP and MPI compile flags. For CUDA it sets nvcc arch 'Kepler Maxwell Pascal' with -Xcompiler -fopenmp -fPIC. No CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or -O level, compiler name or version, or PETSc, Trilinos or CUDA version is recorded in the repo or in docs/benchmarks.rst.
corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/benchmarks.rst (first-party), shared-memory 3D Poisson with 150^3 = 3,375,000 unknowns on dual Xeon E5-2640 v3, CG with smoothed-aggregation AMG: AMGCL sets up the solver about 20-100% faster than Trilinos ML and 4-7x faster than PETSc, and overall CPU performance is on par with Trilinos. Medians computed from the published raw data in docs/smem_data/poisson/{amgcl,trilinos,petsc}.txt (derived from page data): setup on 1 core 3.97 s, against 6.81 s for Trilinos (1.7x) and 27.87 s for PETSc (7.0x); on 16 cores 0.92 s against 1.00 s (1.09x) and 3.57 s (3.9x). Total setup+solve on 1 core 11.58 s against 15.28 s (1.32x) and 49.72 s (4.3x); on 16 cores 2.33 s against 2.48 s (1.06x) and 5.87 s (2.5x). GPU (Tesla K80): AMGCL/CUDA is slightly better than CUSP, and its total time is only about 30% better than CPU AMGCL or Trilinos. Distributed memory: about 3x slower than Trilinos AMG in MareNostrum 4 weak scaling (2.5x faster than Trilinos DD-ML), and 2.5x slower than Trilinos/AMG at 384 cores on SuperMUC.
corrections.caveats: First-party comparison by AMGCL's author. The harness (ddemidov/amgcl_benchmarks) and the raw timing files (docs/smem_data, docs/dmem_data) are public, but compiler, flags, build type and library versions are not recorded anywhere. The hardware is old (Xeon E5-2640 v3, Tesla K80), and the results predate current AMGCL, PETSc and Trilinos releases. The CPU win is mainly in setup time: at 16 cores AMGCL's total is within 6% of Trilinos ML. Each library ran its default smoother (AMGCL SPAI0; Trilinos symmetric Gauss-Seidel; PETSc damped Jacobi), and iteration counts differ widely (AMGCL 24, Trilinos 11, PETSc 7 at 1 core), so this is a defaults-vs-defaults comparison. PETSc scales better than both. In distributed runs AMGCL is about 3x slower than Trilinos AMG in one weak-scaling test and 2.5x slower at 384 cores in another. The GPU speedup is measured against CPU AMGCL, not against a baseline library. The readthedocs page is egress-blocked here; its source docs/benchmarks.rst on GitHub was read instead.
